definition: Indignant means feeling or showing anger at something unjust or unfair.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word indignant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know indignant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Maribel came back to a ticket on the one car on the block with a valid permit, and stood indignant in the street, waving it after the departing scooter.
Annoyed is the small coin of irritation, spent on traffic and slow elevators; indignant is anger with a wrong at the bottom of it.
Incensed goes past indignant — the anger has caught fire and stopped choosing its words.

Outraged is the same anger at unfairness that indignant names, but at full boil and usually at full volume — a public eruption. Indignant keeps its control: the anger has a case to make and is still choosing its words. Outrage erupts; indignant argues.

Offended is the sting of a personal slight — a rude remark, a snub, a joke at your expense — and it is about hurt feelings. Indignant is about injustice: something unfair has been done, and the anger can point to it and argue. You are offended by an insult; you are indignant at a wrong.

Okoye's rhubarb pie was disqualified twenty minutes before judging, for a rule about store-bought crusts that appears nowhere in the printed booklet.
She did not cry and she did not shrug.
Indignant, she stood at the officials' table with the booklet open, reading the rules aloud, slowly, page by page, and asked the head judge to point to the one she had broken.
Indignant is the exact word because it names anger at unfairness in particular.
She isn't merely disappointed at losing, and this isn't a tantrum; the heat comes from the injustice — a rule invented after the fact.
Anger says how she feels; indignant says why the feeling is earned.
Indignant is anger with a case to make: something unfair happened, and the feeling knows it.
Plain angry needs no reason; indignant supplies one.
Its noun is this unit's indignation, and the pair travel together — an indignant customer, full of indignation.
If no injustice is anywhere in sight, the honest word is just annoyed.

Reyna had driven the number 12 bus for nine years without a single late start.
So when the depot posted her name on the tardiness list and docked a day's pay, she did not shout.
She was indignant, and she came to the review board with a folder.
Inside were the gate logs: the depot's own broken gate had held every driver on her route for eleven minutes on each of the mornings in question.
She spoke in an even voice, laid one page at a time on the table, and asked the board to read the timestamps for themselves.
The chairman compared the logs to the list, crossed her name off it, and ordered the docked pay restored.
